cards.explanation: The answer is a great sacrifice. Jehu, king of Israel (2 Kings 9:3), says, “See that no one is missing, for I have a great sacrifice for Baal.” Baal is a false god, so this sounds like the biggest religious event of the year. Just keep your eyes on that word “sacrifice,” friends, because the text is about to tell us what Jehu is really up to.

The answer is that they will not live. Jehu says, “Whoever is missing will not live.” It's a heavy threat. Keep it in mind, friends, because the text tells us right after that Jehu is acting deceptively.

The answer is False. Jehu is not truly planning to serve Baal. The text says it plainly: “But Jehu was acting deceptively in order to destroy the servants of Baal.” The speech about serving Baal a lot is only an act. Jehu is the kind of actor who commits to the part, and I mean COMMITS.

The answer is False. Jehu sent word throughout Israel, and all the servants of Baal came. Not one man stayed home. I'd love to see that attendance record, friends, because I've never gotten a full house in my whole life.

The answer is garments. Jehu says, “Bring out garments for all the servants of Baal.” and the keeper of the wardrobe, the man in charge of the clothing, brings out garments for them. I'd say that's the most organized wardrobe department I've ever heard of, friends.

The answer is servants of the LORD. Jehu tells Baal's servants to look around and see that there are “…no servants of the LORD here among you…” That's the group he names. The check sounds like care for Baal's servants, friends, but the text already told us Jehu is acting deceptively.

The answer is eighty. Jehu had stationed eighty men outside the temple, and he gave them a warning about letting anyone escape. So while the servants of Baal are inside making their offerings, those men are posted outside. That's a lot of men on the job, friends.

The answer is True. Jehu warns his guards, “If anyone allows one of the men I am delivering into your hands to escape, he will forfeit his life for theirs.” He's not leaving room for a small mistake. The eighty men outside know exactly what this job costs if they slip.

The answer is into the inner room of Baal's temple. After they put the servants of Baal to the sword and throw out the bodies, the guards and officers go into the inner room of the temple of Baal. This part of the story is heavy, friends, and I think it's okay to feel that. The text also tells us the temple itself is next on the list.
The answer is burn. The text says, “They brought out the sacred pillar of the temple of Baal and burned it.” That's the end of that pillar, friends. It went up in smoke.
The answer is False. The text says, “Thus Jehu eradicated Baal from Israel…” The servants are gone, the pillars are gone and the temple is torn down. Baal worship doesn't hang on, friends.

The answer is that he doesn't turn away from them. The text says “…he did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit…” Jeroboam was an earlier king of Israel (1 Kings 12:20). The text names those sins as the worship of the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Jehu cleaned out Baal, friends, but he did not turn away from this worship.

The answer is four generations of his sons. The LORD says, “…four generations of your sons will sit on the throne of Israel.” That's the promise after Jehu did well in the LORD's sight and did to the house of Ahab all that was in the LORD's heart. So the throne stays in Jehu's family for a good while, friends.

The answer is True. The text says, “Yet Jehu was not careful to follow the instruction of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart.” He also did not turn away from the sins Jeroboam caused. The text holds both things, friends: the LORD said Jehu did well, and Jehu still wasn't careful with all his heart.

The answer is reduce. The text says, “In those days the LORD began to reduce the size of Israel.” The next verses tell how Hazael, king of Aram (2 Kings 8:13), defeated the Israelites throughout their territory. So Israel starts getting smaller, friends.

The answer is his son Jehoahaz. Jehu rested with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and his son Jehoahaz reigned in his place. That fits with the LORD's promise that Jehu's sons would sit on the throne (2 Kings 10:30). The throne stays in the family, friends.

The answer is twenty-eight. The text says the duration of Jehu's reign over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years. That's a long stretch on the throne, friends. Nearly three decades of the same king.
